To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cosmic star formation rate peaks around z ∼ 4 in the blue (i.e. at the epoch of peak galaxy formation rate) and that it rises to about 10 times its present value at the far-infrared (i.e. the epoch of peak dust-obscured star formation).
the star formation rate in elliptical galaxies increases with redshift, peaks at z ∼ 4 and then declines.

the cosmic star formation history, the cosmic background radiation and galaxy counts and redhift distributions can be explained in terms of the hierarchical clustering scenario for galaxy formation and a simple model of galaxy interactions that is based on a few free parameters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new approach for modelling galaxy formation in which galaxy interactions are the main driving force for the evolution of galaxies along the Hubble classification.
the evolution of galaxies in a hierarchical clustering universe and the role of galaxy–galaxy interactions in shaping the Hubble sequence.

the following issues: (1) the origin of the cosmic star formation history (2) the origin of galaxy morphology and the origin of the Hubble sequence (3) the origin of diffuse background radiation (4) the origin of infrared galaxies and (5) the origin of submillimetre galaxies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model is able to reproduce the statistical properties of galaxy populations and their evolution over the entire Hubble time.
the Press-Schechter formalism coupled with a simple prescription for the evolution of galaxy interactions is capable of reproducing the observed galaxy properties in a wide range of wavelengths.

the Press‐Schecter model, coupled with galaxy–galaxy interactions, is capable of reproducing the statistical and morphological properties of galaxies and of making reliable multiwavelength predictions of the star formation history, the cosmic star formation rate and the diffuse background.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the collision-induced galaxy formation model can reproduce a wide variety of observational data and can be used to make predictions for the evolution of galaxies as a function of type.

the model predicts the evolution in the number density and spectral energy distribution of galaxies as well, and is therefore a powerful tool to interpret the results of deep surveys at different wavelengths.
the Press‐Schaechter formalism is very powerful in explaining the observed properties of galaxies, but only when coupled to a prescription for galaxy–galaxy interactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a model based on a single set of physical parameters is able to reproduce a large variety of observations.
the Press‐Shechter formalism, coupled with a simple prescription for the evolution of galaxy interactions, is able to account for the main features observed in the galaxy population.

the evolution of galaxies is dominated by their internal processes, such as the formation and destruction of discs and bulges and the star formation history, which are not directly affected by the large-scale environment.
